articles.title: Alerta por dengue en La Libertad: Minsa reporta más de 10 mil casos en lo que va del 2026
articles.summary: La Libertad suma 10 454 casos de dengue en 2026, frente a los 200 registrados en el mismo periodo de 2025. El Minsa reporta tres fallecidos.
articles.body_text: La Libertad registra 10.454 casos de dengue en lo que va de 2026, según la última actualización del Ministerio de Salud (Minsa). La cifra representa un incremento considerable frente al mismo periodo de 2025, cuando la región reportó solo 200 casos de esta enfermedad transmitida por la picadura del mosquito Aedes aegypti. Además, las autoridades sanitarias informaron que tres personas fallecieron por dengue en la región liberteña. Los decesos se registraron en las provincias de Virú, Pacasmayo y Trujillo, de acuerdo con la información proporcionada. De acuerdo con los datos del Minsa, la provincia de Trujillo concentra la mayor cantidad de casos sospechosos de dengue, con 5.667. En segundo lugar se encuentra Virú, con 3.032 casos. También se han reportado casos en las provincias de Chepén, Pacasmayo y Ascope, lo que mantiene en alerta a las autoridades sanitarias ante la propagación de la enfermedad en distintos puntos de la región. La comparación con 2025 evidencia un aumento marcado de los contagios reportados: de 200 casos en el mismo periodo del año pasado a 10.454 en lo que va de 2026. El Minsa informó que las tres víctimas mortales procedían de Virú, Pacasmayo y Trujillo. Según la información difundida por RPP, las personas fallecidas se habrían automedicado y no acudieron oportunamente a un establecimiento de salud. A diferencia de este año, durante el mismo periodo de 2025 La Libertad no había registrado fallecimientos por dengue, según los datos proporcionados. Ante la presencia de síntomas compatibles con la enfermedad, es importante evitar la automedicación y acudir a un centro de salud para recibir una evaluación médica oportuna. Como parte de su plan de contingencia, el Ministerio de Salud desarrolla estrategias de prevención que incluyen campañas de concientización y vacunación, de acuerdo con la información proporcionada. Las acciones buscan reducir el riesgo de transmisión y reforzar la protección de la población. También se ha señalado que algunas personas se niegan a permitir el ingreso del personal sanitario a sus viviendas, lo que dificulta las intervenciones preventivas. Por ello, las autoridades insisten en la importancia de facilitar las labores del personal de salud y mantener las medidas de control del mosquito transmisor. articles.title: Machu Picchu: gremios turísticos respaldan eliminar el plazo de tres horas para comprar entradas
articles.summary: Gremios turísticos respaldan eliminar el plazo de tres horas para comprar entradas a Machu Picchu y plantean cambios urgentes en la plataforma.
articles.body_text: Los principales gremios del sector turismo expresaron su respaldo a la eliminación del plazo de tres horas para concretar la compra de entradas a Machu Picchu. Sin embargo, solicitaron al Ministerio de Cultura implementar mejoras urgentes en la plataforma de venta de boletos para garantizar un proceso transparente, seguro y accesible para visitantes y operadores turísticos formales. En un pronunciamiento conjunto difundido en Cusco este viernes 9 de octubre, las organizaciones señalaron que la modernización del sistema debe asegurar la disponibilidad real de entradas y condiciones equitativas para los distintos usuarios. Las organizaciones precisaron que no respaldan el retorno a mecanismos que permitan retener cupos durante periodos prolongados sin que se haya efectuado el pago correspondiente. También aclararon que solicitar cambios operativos no significa rechazar de manera general la plataforma de venta. En ese sentido, sostuvieron que las decisiones técnicas deben responder a criterios objetivos y no a presiones para recuperar procedimientos que consideran superados. Los firmantes remarcaron que el objetivo es contar con un sistema moderno que responda a las necesidades del sector turístico. Los gremios solicitaron al Ministerio de Cultura, entidad responsable de administrar la plataforma, habilitar funcionalidades diferenciadas para visitantes individuales y operadores turísticos formales. Entre las medidas propuestas figuran herramientas para gestionar múltiples reservas, realizar operaciones por lotes, garantizar la trazabilidad de las transacciones y agilizar los pagos mediante procedimientos seguros y verificables. Asimismo, advirtieron sobre la necesidad de establecer una solución operativa oportuna y previsible para la venta diferida y continua de entradas correspondientes al 2027, especialmente para el Camino Inca. En el documento, las organizaciones señalaron que los costos y riesgos de la transición tecnológica no deben trasladarse indebidamente a los usuarios ni a las empresas turísticas. Por ello, plantearon habilitar diversas alternativas de pago, sin limitar las opciones a las tarjetas de crédito, además de revisar el impacto de las comisiones sobre los operadores. También solicitaron garantizar una capacidad tecnológica suficiente, soporte oportuno y protocolos de contingencia frente a eventuales caídas de la plataforma, errores del sistema o pagos no procesados. Los gremios advirtieron que la etapa de marcha blanca no debe convertirse en una operación permanente que mantenga limitaciones conocidas. Otro de los pedidos consiste en que el Ministerio de Cultura y el Ministerio de Comercio Exterior y Turismo (Mincetur) presenten de manera conjunta y pública un cronograma verificable de mejoras. Este deberá incluir responsables, plazos de implementación y mecanismos de seguimiento con participación de las organizaciones del sector. El pronunciamiento fue suscrito por instituciones como la Asociación de Agencias de Turismo del Cusco, la Asociación Peruana de Operadores de Turismo Receptivo e Interno (Apotur), la Asociación Peruana de Agencias de Viajes y Turismo (Apavit), la Cámara Regional de Turismo del Cusco, la Cámara de Comercio del Cusco y la Cámara Nacional de Turismo del Perú (Canatur), entre otras. También figuran ComexPerú, el Colegio Profesional de Licenciados en Turismo de la región Cusco y organizaciones de guías turísticos. Finalmente, los firmantes reafirmaron su compromiso con la atención a los visitantes y la competitividad de Machu Picchu como destino turístico. En su pronunciamiento, sostuvieron que la solución no es retroceder, sino garantizar una plataforma moderna, accesible, segura y adecuada a las distintas modalidades de comercialización turística.

articles.body_text: Temblor de magnitud 4.2 remeció esta mañana, viernes 9 de octubre, la región Arequipa. De acuerdo con el reporte sísmico del Instituto Geofísico del Perú (IGP), el movimiento telúrico se registró exactamente a las 5:55 a.m. El epicentro tuvo lugar a 33 kilómetros al sureste de la localidad de Aplao, provincia de Castilla, alcanzando una profundidad de 107 kilómetros. Debido a su profundidad intermedia, el sismo fue percibido de manera leve en diversos sectores de la provincia y zonas adyacentes. Hasta el momento, el Instituto Nacional de Defensa Civil (INDECI) no reporta daños materiales ni personas afectadas. Cabe recordar que el Perú se encuentra ubicado en una zona de alta actividad sísmica, conocida como el Cinturón de Fuego del Pacífico. Esta franja concentra gran parte de los movimientos telúricos del mundo debido al constante roce entre las placas tectónicas, por lo que los especialistas recomiendan mantener medidas de prevención. De acuerdo a la información brindada y compartida por Indeci, estos son los artículos, productos e implementos que toda mochila de emergencia debe contener: alimentos no perecibles como atún, galletas soda, frutos secos, caramelos, botellas de agua, dinero en monedas, artículos específicos para bebés e infantes, entre otros. También botiquín de primeros auxilios (vendas, gasas, esparadrapo, mascarillas, agua oxigenada, crema tópica, analgésicos, antibióticos), bolsas plásticas de basura, mantas, cuerdas y artículos de comunicación como linterna, radio o silbato.

articles.title: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Orkut's founder is now taking aim at algorithms and AI-generated content.
articles.body_text: Orkut , the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection. In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join. Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube. In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote. “I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added. This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users . In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch. Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch. articles.title: Exclusive: Automattic loses its interim CFO just weeks after boardroom shakeup
articles.summary: Automattic's interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left the company less than a month after taking the role, TechCrunch has learned. Sources say his departure followed a demotion back to his previous position, marking another executive exit amid the organization's leadership turmoil.
articles.body_text: Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired. The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.” Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit. He was meant to replace the former CFO, Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean. Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan. A source at Automattic told TechCrunch that Klaperman was upset the board was considering external candidates for the CFO role. Though he was announced internally as interim CFO, the board never legally approved his title, the source said. In addition, there was a disagreement with Mullenweg over a work project related to employee performance reviews, which led to Mullenweg’s demotion of Klaperman back to his former position at VIP. Klaperman resigned shortly thereafter. Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure. The company is still performing an external search for a qualified CFO candidate, we understand. After publication, the company issued a statement via X post , which implies that Klaperman was offended by the board’s search for external CFO candidates. It read, “At Automattic, we consider it best practice to evaluate external candidates for critical roles alongside internal people stepping up. articles.title: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Flock would not say if CEO Garrett Langley would take a pay cut following the reduction in workforce.
articles.body_text: Surveillance camera maker Flock is cutting its workforce as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology. News of the staff cuts comes from Reuters, which reported that Flock is reducing its staff by 18%, or around 270 employees, across the board. The publication said the employees are leaving at the end of October following a voluntary buyout program. Wired reported last month that Flock was asking some of its employees to leave, citing the need to shrink its staff to avoid mandatory layoffs. Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel told TechCrunch in a statement on Friday: “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth. This was a voluntary program, not a layoff, and reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.” Flock’s spokesperson would not comment further when asked by TechCrunch if chief executive Garrett Langley or other executives took a pay cut as part of the program. Flock has faced heavy criticism and mounting pushback from communities across the United States and legislators looking to rein in the company’s privately run mass surveillance program . Flock has installed over 100,000 license plate-reading cameras across the U.S., which allow police and federal agents to track the location and whereabouts of vehicles passing by them. Dozens of police officers have been arrested , fired, or forced to resign for abusing access to Flock’s system to search, track, and stalk people without a warrant or their permission. While some cities have moved to take down Flock’s cameras citing public outcry, Flock quickly replaced them, prompting some Americans to destroy the cameras . Flock has also been criticized for its poor cybersecurity, including allowing cameras to be publicly exposed and accessible from the web . Security experts have questioned Flock’s accuracy after the system has misidentified license plates, resulting in improper police stops and arrests, including a journalist who was driving an authorized review vehicle. articles.body_text: With over a thousand emails, slides, texts, and documents unveiled during the United States v. Elizabeth Holmes trial, Extend engineer Bo Lau created a website that simulates what it might have been like to be the chief executive of Theranos before everything came crashing down. (Every day, I am grateful to the American legal system for making the discovery process public.) i built a website where you can sit at elizabeth holmes’ desk open her macbook, scroll her iphone, run the theranos edison machine her texts, emails, slides, documents, and theranos machine records are real, sourced from exhibits in the united states v. holmes criminal trial pic.twitter.com/5At9T5m3UV The environment that Lau created is ambitiously detailed, taking you right back to 2016, a time when iPhones had home buttons, and you had to slide your finger across the screen to unlock it. Even the MacBook Air is running OS X El Capitan. You can click around the environment, which lets you look through the documents made public from the court case on Holmes’ iPhone and laptop screens. You can even run the Theranos Edison machine, the company’s ill-fated device that was supposed to be able to extract large amounts of health data from one drop of blood. The project seems like it was mostly made for laughs, but it’s actually an interesting way to peruse the documents from one of the most infamous court cases in tech history — it’s a lot easier to navigate this than to source thousands of PDFs from court websites. There’s another agenda, though. Lau is promoting a watch party that her company is throwing for Nathan Fielder’s upcoming documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, “ You Can See Everything .” Also, of course, she’s promoting the company itself. So, what exactly does Extend do? Apparently, it can “parse, extract, and split your hardest documents with unmatched accuracy.” (I’m not really sure what that means, but if it makes something like this Holmes desk simulator possible, then I guess that means I’m bullish on B2B SaaS.) articles.summary: Three fired OpenAI safety researchers dispute allegations of mishandling sensitive information, warning in an open letter that their dismissals are creating a chilling effect on the company’s AI safety culture.
articles.body_text: Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak, and Mikita Balesni, the three safety researchers that OpenAI fired last week , have published an open letter denying the firm’s claims that they mishandled sensitive information outside of established company procedures and warned that their dismissal signals a chilling effect that will have ripple effects across the company’s culture. “We have become concerned that internal and external communications around our firing have made our former colleagues afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI,” the researchers wrote Thursday in an open letter to OpenAI’s Safety and Security Committee, Safety Advisory Group, and Mission Advisory Council. The researchers were dismissed last week after allegedly sharing confidential company information with a third-party AI safety organization. OpenAI said they violated the company’s policies by “accessing and handling sensitive company information.” “AI is not a normal technology, and OpenAI is not a normal company,” Wang, Korbak, and Balesni wrote. “Those of us who work on safety see risks before anyone else, and we rely on close collaboration with outside experts to work out how to address them. The freedom to do so without fear, and to have well-defined internal procedures that enable this work, is itself an essential safety mechanism.” They said that their firing represents a broader shift in the culture of OpenAI, one that used to encourage workers to “raise safety concerns and disagree openly.” They said employees are now “unclear on where they stand” when behavior that was allegedly normal a month ago is now suddenly grounds for dismissal. “Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they wrote. “Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.” In the letter, the three denied involvement in a leak to The Information about less monitorable architectures in OpenAI’s newest models that make chain-of-thought reasoning more difficult to monitor. They also denied engaging with external parties outside the mandates of their jobs. OpenAI has not formally responded to the open letter, but shared with TechCrunch an internal memo attributed to a research leader, praising the three researchers’ contributions to AI safety and denying that they were fired in retaliation. “I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the memo reads. “We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns.” Separately, an OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch the three were fired after an investigation revealed a “pattern of misconduct” in “clear violation of our policies of mishandling research information” that goes beyond sharing information with an outside AI evaluation group. OpenAI did not directly address TechCrunch’s questions about specifically which policies the researchers allegedly violated, the circumstances of their dismissal, or how the company protects employees who raise safety concerns and collaborate with external evaluators. The firings have fueled speculation about their circumstances, particularly as OpenAI faces scrutiny over recent safety incidents involving rogue agents and leaks about its models.

articles.title: Ben Affleck is an AI nerd, and the internet is impressed | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Ben Affleck is going viral for his deep knowledge of AI, from neural networks and transformers to open weights. The actor, who sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix earlier this year, is proving he's more than just a Hollywood star.
articles.body_text: They cast the wrong lead in “Good Will Hunting,” apparently, because it’s Ben Affleck who is the secret genius, as it turns out. The actor who earlier this year sold his AI filmmaking startup to Netflix for a reported $587 million has gone viral this week for demonstrating his understanding of AI technology, neural networks, machine learning, and the like, across multiple video clips of his recent interviews. He can even write a little Python, he says. The movie star delved into his interest in technology most recently on an episode of GQ’s “One More Question” series this week, where he humbly started with “I’ve always been kind of into computers since I was young,” before nerding out on the development of AI as it relates to filmmaking, while using AI terminology like machine learning, neural networks, transformers, tensors, GPUs, inference, and more. In a clip that’s making the rounds, Affleck explains to the impressed interviewer, Zach Baron, that he got into the space when analog film moved to digital. As he spoke, he kept defining terms so the interviewer could understand what he was talking about. “I became more interested in that aspect of it, and the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning,” Affleck began. “So I can write, like, pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that. Because with convolutional neural networks — which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do — which is just much more computation simultaneously — you would do things like, look at what’s called a tensor — which is just the numerical translation of a visual image, in numbers like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame, and how many? It’s just that simple, right?” No, Ben Affleck, it is not just that simple, which is why this video is going viral. The actor then went into how neural networks were used to identify patterns and do edge detection or feature extraction, which he described as “identifying patterns enough to know — like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.” He also admitted he used his status as a Hollywood star to get a peek at emerging AI technology, at times. OpenAI was among those he visited, Affleck said in a separate clip, which ultimately led him to understand how he could get more directly involved in the AI space. As the interviewer continued, Affleck explained how AI can help with filmmaking while not replacing it, leading to the development and sale of his own startup in this space. (He claims the $587 million figure is “not right,” noting that he didn’t own the whole company.) “I gambled on this notion that in order to do this in an ethical way and in a way that could take this technology and actually make it work hand in glove with artists in this community where there are very fixed, long-standing relationships around likeness and so forth, we had to create our own dataset,” he said. “So I raised the money. I shot for about eight months with a lot of cameras and a lot of equipment, and created a dataset that would serve as late-stage training for open models to do discrete tasks, sort of where the training code, the inference code, were related to one another and geared toward actual specific tasks that would generate value,” Affleck said. In a separate clip, also going viral, Affleck spoke to Bloomberg’s Lucas Shaw at the Screentime 2026 conference in LA, where he talked about how he fine-tuned AI models by taking open source models, unfreezing the weights, then teaching them to meet certain cinematic standards. In the process, the filmmaker retains their proprietary work, while benefiting from the learning they create by training their own unique model for the movie they’re making. articles.title: OpenAI's math solutions aren't meeting the field's standards yet | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI's flood of proofs deviated from the guidelines set by a group of mathematical researchers consulted by the frontier lab.
articles.body_text: When OpenAI released hundreds of claimed solutions to some of the world’s hardest math problems this week, the frontier lab said that it had consulted an advisory group of elite mathematicians to avoid the controversy that came with the last time one of its models solved a long-standing problem in the field. But OpenAI fell short of those standards, particularly where the mathematicians emphasized the need for human understanding of a mathematical result. That’s especially concerning after a new paper highlighted gaps between the natural language and formally expressed solution to a million-dollar problem ostensibly solved by OpenAI’s models. The Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), hosted by the Institute for Advanced Study, is made up of nine prominent researchers at institutions around the world. The organization released guidelines for frontier labs solving math problems at the end of September. In a statement on the latest set of proofs, the AGMAI said that “it is ultimately up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully.” However, the organization’s first request was “to stop testing advanced mathematical problems on proprietary models.” OpenAI’s release explicitly says that it is evaluating its proprietary models using open research problems in mathematics. The advisory group did not respond when asked by TechCrunch for a more thorough evaluation of OpenAI’s latest proof release. The lab clearly followed some of its principles, including releasing results as soon as possible and including information about how the models reached their conclusions. But not for all of them: Just 10 of the 719 manuscripts included releases of the model’s chain of thought. For papers that people don’t understand, the mathematicians suggested the proofs should be formalized — but just 42% of the proofs released by OpenAI had not undergone this process. Ultimately, it’s still not clear that OpenAI is taking “responsibility for ensuring that human understanding will follow” when releasing its proofs, in accordance to the AGMAI principles. AGMAI suggested that OpenAI should help fund the work of human mathematicians who will be required to make the lab’s solutions meaningful in any real way. “Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field itself once their initial target is ‘solved’, and do not understand the AI output well enough to answer questions on the result, give talks, or otherwise interact with the rest of the field,” Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician who has criticized OpenAI’s approach, wrote on social media after the release. That problem is exemplified by a paper released this week by mathematicians at the University of Cambridge and King’s College in London that questions the way frontier labs are approaching these challenges. When AI models solve mathematical problems, they first create a “natural language” explanation, then try to express that result in Lean, a programming language that in theory confirms the accuracy of the proof by compiling it as code. However, there may be problems with the way the models translate their natural language proofs into code; this paper documents at least two discrepancies between the natural language proof and the Lean code behind the solution OpenAI has offered to a problem derived from the Navier-Stokes equations that describe the complex behavior of fluids.

articles.title: Not even Spotify is safe from AI slop
articles.summary: Artists such as Standards, Health, Annie, and Swans have had AI-generated albums that aren’t theirs showing up on their Spotify pages. Why?
articles.body_text: I first noticed something weird when a HEALTH album dropped on my Spotify new release radar. Except the cover design was funny — it didn’t look like a HEALTH album. And it wasn’t. [Image: A screenshot of the fake Annie album, taken October 12th. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25732450/Screenshot_2024_10_12_at_4.23.09_PM.png?quality=90&strip=all] Some kind of AI slop had been uploaded to HEALTH’s artist page on Spotify, one of three fake albums that would appear under their name that weekend. The band’s X account made some jokes about it, the albums were eventually removed, and I went back to minding my own business. Then, the next weekend, I saw a new Annie album had dropped. That album was more plausible — Annie had just released a new single, “The Sky Is Blue” — but when I clicked in, I couldn’t find it on the list of the song titles. Confused, I played the album and heard birdsong and a vaguely New Age-y instrumental. That… did not sound like Annie. So I did what any normal person would do: I bitched about it in my group chat. Which was how I heard that this was happening to other artists, like a lot of artists, and had been happening for months. (“I get one of these in my release radar often,” my buddy Gordon said.) For a while, metalcore artists such as Caliban, Northlane, and Silent Planet had been targeted. But so had a lot of artists with single-word names, such as Swans, Asia, Standards, and Gong. A new album would appear on an artist’s Spotify page, bearing their name but no similarity to their music. Sometimes, as with the fake HEALTH albums, they would disappear after a few days. Other times, they would linger indefinitely, even against the artist’s will. [Image: Can you spot the fake? https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25732455/Screenshot_2024_10_15_at_12.48.26_PM.png?quality=90&strip=all] “It was super weird,” says Marcos Mena, Standards’ lead songwriter and guitarist. “I thought, ‘Oh, this is something Spotify will take care of.’” After all, Standards has a verified artist page. But when a fake album was posted on September 26th, it didn’t budge. Mena emailed Spotify to tell them there’d been a mistake. The streamer responded two weeks later, on October 8th: “It looks like the content is mapped correctly to the artist’s page. If you require further assistance, please contact your music provider. Please do not reply to this message.” As of November 8th, the fake Standards album was still right there under the band’s verified, blue-checked name. It was finally removed by November 11th. “That was upsetting to me, because if you have ears, you can definitely hear it’s not our music,” Mena told me. “It’s definitely a bummer because we did have a new album come out this year, and I feel like it’s detracting from that.” What if someone came to a concert where Standards was opening for another band, went to Spotify to check out more tunes, and got the fake album instead? [Image: Can you spot the fake? https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25732473/Screenshot_2024_11_08_at_3.26.43_PM.png?quality=90&strip=all] To me, this all raised an obvious question: fucking why? Given the history of scams on Spotify, I think the answer is money. (The answer is almost always money.) To understand how this works, you need a sense of the mechanics. Streaming platforms like Spotify don’t work like your Facebook page — Mena and other artists aren’t logging in and adding albums to their accounts directly. Instead, they go through a distributor that handles licensing, metadata, and royalty payments. Distributors send songs and metadata in bulk to the streaming services. The metadata part is important; it includes things such as the song title and artist name but also other information, such as the songwriter, record label, and so on. This is crucial for artists (and others) to get paid. But this whole process effectively works on the honor system, and for something like the fake Standards album, this is where the problems begin. A distributor takes you at your word that you are who you say you are, Spotify takes the distributor at their word, and boom, there’s a fake album on a real artist’s page. Most of the time when this happens, it’s an honest mistake. In the recent spate of fakes, though, it seems like artists are directly targeted. Because the money an artist receives for streams goes through the distributor, the fake Standards album — should it get any payout at all — will reward someone other than Mena. We know the real Standards are on Topshelf Records, but the fake appears to be on something called Gupta Music, so Standards’ real label isn’t getting a cut, either. If enough people stream the album, the royalties will flow straight to Gupta Music… along with the payout from hundreds of other releases full of slop. Mena said he’d filed with his distributor to have the fake Standards album taken down. But whoever did it — Spotify or his distributor — didn’t notify Mena; I did, when I asked if he’d been involved in the removal. He wasn’t, he texted me, “but yayyyyy someone did something.” Going to Every Noise at Once — essentially an encyclopedia of what’s on Spotify — and searching for Gupta Music, I saw more than 700 releases. The cover art looked remarkably similar and smacked of AI. The purported band names were mostly one word: “Rany,” “Living,” “Bedroom,” and “Culture.” The albums shared names with the faux bands. A search for “Gupta Music” returned only a 14-year-old TED Talk by a man named Robert Gupta. [Image: Screenshot of Every Noise at Once, before the albums were removed. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/25732478/Screenshot_2024_10_31_at_1.36.06_PM.png?quality=90&strip=all] Even the supposed label name struck me as suspicious. There’s a well-known marketing agency called Gupta Media. It reps entertainment companies including Disney Music Group, Republic Records (in service of The Weeknd’s album), and Sony Music. In an email to The Verge, Gupta Media spokesperson Carly Carioli confirmed the agency “has no connection” to Gupta Music. “To be clear, Gupta Media is not now nor have we ever been involved in any of the activity you’re addressing — i.e., uploading fake music by fake artists to the profiles of real artists,” said Carioli. It looks like Standards, Annie, HEALTH, Swans, and a number of other notable one-word artists were targeted directly. Spotify confirmed that the onslaught of AI garbage was delivered from one source, the licensor Ameritz Music. Ameritz Music did not respond to a request for comment. “Due to significant and repeated violations of Spotify’s Metadata Style Guide, we ended our relationship with the licensor that provided the content in question,” said Chris Macowski, Spotify’s global head of music communication, in an emailed statement. “As a result, the content was removed from our platform.” Macowski also said that Spotify “invests heavily in automated and manual reviews” to prevent royalty fraud. Earlier attempts focused on metalcore musicians such as Fit for an Autopsy, Alpha Wolf, and Like Moths to Flames also seem like a coordinated attempt to siphon off legitimate streams. The culprit in that case was Vibratech Musicians, according to Idioteq. Each individual payout for a song stream on Spotify is tiny, as legitimate musicians who use the platform frequently lament. But hundreds or thousands of songs with relatively modest streaming numbers, when combined, can lead to big payouts. A fraudster just has to upload music and find a way to make accounts play it. And this doesn’t just happen on Spotify. There are more than 100 streaming platforms where artists can run this scam. In early November, Universal Music Group (UMG) sued Believe, a music distributor, and its US subsidiary TuneCore. In that lawsuit, UMG alleges Believe has a “conscious business strategy of indiscriminately distributing and purporting to license tracks with full knowledge that many of the clients of its distribution services are fraudsters.” The suit is about copyright infringement, and the details in it are striking. UMG alleges that artists such as “Kendrik Laamar,” “Arriana Gramde,” “Jutin Biber,” and “Llady Gaga” are among those Believe uploaded — suggesting a strategy of attempting to capture streams from users who had simply typoed. Another strategy is creating AI covers of popular songs and getting them onto popular playlists so normal people will stream them. Another involves bots “listening” to songs. Earlier this year, a Danish man was sentenced to 18 months in prison for using bots to get about $300,000 in royalties. Another man, Michael Smith, was arrested and charged with defrauding streaming services out of $10 million over the course of seven years. Smith used AI tools to create hundreds of thousands of songs under the names of fake artists such as “Calm Baseball,” “Calm Connected,” and “Calm Knuckles.” He then streamed the huge catalog using bots, billions of times, prosecutors allege. That diverted money that should have gone to real musicians that real people were really listening to. (In this case, Spotify paid only $60,000 to Smith, suggesting the company’s protective measures worked to limit payments, Macowski said.) “People upload massive amounts of albums that are intended to be streaming fraud albums,” says Andrew Batey, the CEO of Beatdapp, a company that aims to prevent streaming fraud. Batey estimates that $2 billion to $3 billion is stolen from artists through this kind of fraud every year. Distribution plays a big role. Most distributors’ business models are based on getting a cut of whatever royalties come back to the artists and labels. “Even though they may not be participating in the fraud, they directly benefit from it,” Batey says. In its suit, UMG alleges that Believe “wrongfully collects royalties it knows are properly payable by digital music services” such as UMG on copyrighted material. A sophisticated fraud operation will use multiple fake labels and multiple distributors in order to avoid having a single point of failure. Besides bot accounts, a number of bad actors have access to real people’s compromised accounts. “They log in as you and me, play their song three times and leave,” Batey says. That fake stream is then hidden among all the real listening the real account is doing. Gupta Music wasn’t the only label I found doing bulk uploading. There were three more doing something similar: Future Jazz Records, Ancient Lake Records, and Beat Street Music. All had also uploaded hundreds of albums with AI-looking album art. It’s unclear how these labels intended to generate streams, if at all. By the time of publication, most of those albums had been removed. Problems with metadata have existed for years — some of them innocent, some considerably less so. “We’ve basically gotten lucky so far,” says Glenn McDonald, a former Spotify employee who runs Every Noise at Once. “The content validation system without any input on the artist level is fairly crazy.” When something goes wrong, there are two levels where it can be addressed: the streaming service and the distributor. Distributors have to strike a delicate balance. They make their money by getting a cut of the streaming payout. If they are too aggressive in policing the uploads, legitimate artists get caught. Fixing that is expensive, and distribution is a low-margin, bulk business, McDonald says. But allowing too many junk bands through creates problems with the streaming services. As for the streaming services, they usually have data that could allow them to sort this out. If, for instance, the distributor that usually uploads Standards albums isn’t the one used for the new album, that’s the kind of thing that could be used to flag the album for review. (So is the change in label.) McDonald told me he also built tools for Spotify to identify when a song doesn’t sound like the rest of an artist’s catalog. Sometimes that can happen for legitimate reasons; an EDM remix of an Ed Sheeran song isn’t going to sound like Ed Sheeran, but it may still have happened with the label’s and artist’s approval. Also, some legitimate artists share the same name, especially tiny indie bands, and they just have separate pages. “The way it should have worked, getting the plumbing right, is that all those albums should have been flagged as new artists, and then it wouldn’t matter,” McDonald told me. As for the distributors, the thing to keep an eye on is UMG’s lawsuit. A pretrial conference is scheduled for January. The outcome of the suit could potentially change how distributors filter the music people try to upload through their platforms — because if lawsuits are more expensive than content moderation, there’s likely to be more content moderation. That could improve things for Spotify, which is downstream of them. Just banning AI-generated content from Spotify — or distributors — might feel like an intuitive solution. But despite the backlash against AI-generated media, there are legitimate AI-generated songs. For instance, “10 Drunk Cigarettes,” from Girly Girl Productions, is something of a hit. (It also is likely human-assisted, rather than wholly AI-generated.) UMG has made a deal with Soundlabs to allow artists to use Soundlabs’ AI vocals for themselves. It’s also partnered with Klay Vision to create a model for generating music. Besides, AI is just an accelerant for a type of fraud that’s lived on Spotify for years, says Batey. Fraudsters used to dig up old, obscure albums and digitize them or slightly alter a song that already existed. AI has just cut down on the amount of work that’s required to make the fake song needed to get the streaming money. At the same time… accelerants sure do make things burn down faster. Plenty of platforms have become less useful as they’ve been choked with AI glurge — Facebook, Instagram, the artist formerly known as Twitter, even Google itself. AI music poses the same threat to Spotify, McDonald says. He points out that I had been waiting for the Annie album, excited for it, even. And then instead, I got duped into garbage. “There’s all these mechanisms around assuming this stuff is correct,” he says. But right now, those mechanisms are broken — and people who truly care, like artists themselves, don’t have their hands on the controls. Update November 15th: Adds emailed statement from Gupta Media. Correction November 15th: The original version of this story referred to Carly Carioli as a spokeswoman. Carioli uses he/him pronouns.

articles.title: Google’s invisible AI watermark will help identify generative text and video
articles.summary: Google DeepMind’s SynthID can now watermark AI-generated video and text. It’s one of several standards alongside C2PA.
articles.body_text: Among Google’s swath of new AI models and tools announced today, the company is also expanding its AI content watermarking and detection technology to work across two new mediums. Google’s DeepMind CEO, Demis Hassabis, took the stage for the first time at the Google I/O developer conference on Tuesday to talk not only about the team’s new AI tools, like the Veo video generator, but also about the new upgraded SynthID watermark imprinting system. It can now mark video that was digitally generated as well as AI-generated text. Watermarking AI-generated content will matter increasingly as the technology gains prevalence, especially when AI gets used for malicious purposes. It’s already been used to spread political misinformation, claim someone said something they haven’t, and create nonconsensual sexual content. SynthID was announced last August and started as a tool to imprint AI imagery in a way that humans can’t visually decipher — but can be detected by the system. The approach is different from other aspiring watermarking protocol standards like C2PA, which adds cryptographic metadata to AI-generated content. Google had also enabled SynthID to inject inaudible watermarks into AI-generated music that was made using DeepMind’s Lyria model. SynthID is just one of several AI safeguards in development to combat misuse by the tech, safeguards that the Biden administration is directing federal agencies to build guidelines around. articles.title: The FCC bans robocalls with AI-generated voices
articles.summary: The Federal Communications Commission has banned the use of AI-generated voices in robocalls. A ruling issued on Thursday makes the voices illegal.
articles.body_text: The Federal Communications Commission is making it illegal for robocalls to use AI-generated voices. The ruling, issued on Thursday, gives state attorneys general the ability to take action against callers using AI voice cloning tech. As outlined in the ruling, AI-generated voices are now considered “an artificial or prerecorded voice” under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA). This restricts callers from using AI-generated voices for non-emergency purposes or without prior consent. The TCPA includes bans on a variety of automated call practices, including using an “artificial or prerecorded voice” to deliver messages, but it wasn’t explicitly stated whether this included AI-powered voice cloning. The new ruling clarifies that these recordings should indeed fall under the law’s scope. “Bad actors are using AI-generated voices in unsolicited robocalls to extort vulnerable family members, imitate celebrities, and misinform voters,” FCC Chairwoman Jessica Rosenworcel said in a statement. “State Attorneys General will now have new tools to crack down on these scams and ensure the public is protected from fraud and misinformation.” Although state attorneys general could already go after the bad actors behind robocalls based on the scam or fraud they’re perpetrating, this new ruling gives them the power to hold scam artists accountable solely because they’re using an AI-generated voice. The FCC first proposed banning the use of AI voices in robocalls last month. Scrutiny of AI voices in robocalls has ramped up in recent weeks. In January, some New Hampshire residents received a call that appeared to use AI to impersonate President Joe Biden’s voice, and it told them not to show up at the polls for the state’s presidential primary. An investigation has since linked the robocall to two Texas-based companies: Life Corporation and Lingo Telecom. The FCC issued a cease-and-desist order to Lingo Telecom, which transmitted the call.

articles.title: Daniel, 18, dog i busskraschen – familjens sorg
articles.summary: Daniel Bratis, 18, gillade fotboll, att umgås med familj och vänner och bygga lego med sin lillebror. Men i måndags kom han aldrig hem från skolan. ”Hans frånvaro har lämnat ett tomrum i våra liv som ingenting någonsin kan fylla”, skriver hans familj till Expressen.

Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Omkring 40 personer, däribland många skolungdomar, befann sig ombord på dubbeldäckarbussen som körde av vägen och välte mellan Växjö och Alvesta i måndags eftermiddag. Ett tiotal skadades och fördes till sjukhus. En passagerare, 18-årige Daniel Bratis, överlevde inte. Han var på väg hem till Ljungby från Växjö, där han gick i gymnasiet. ”Vi är förkrossade. Daniel var vår son, och han hade hela livet framför sig. Det finns helt enkelt inga ord som kan beskriva smärtan i att förlora ett barn”, skriver de i ett uttalande. Det är Daniels mamma Monica Bratis, pappa Vasile Cristian Bratis, lillebror Andrei Catalin Bratis och kusinen Nicolae Bogdan Bratis, på tillfälligt besök från Skottland, som uttalar sig gemensamt. Familjen kommer från Rumänien. För ett par år sen flyttade de till Sverige och slog sig ner i Ljungby. Daniel började på IB-programmet på Katedralskolan i Växjö, en knapp timmes bussfärd från Ljungby. IB står för International Baccalaureate och är en utbildning på engelska, för elever som planerar att studera eller arbeta utomlands. Vid sidan av skolan arbetade han extra åt ett solcellsföretag. Familjen beskriver honom som en positiv och glad ung man, full av liv och ambitioner.

articles.title: Expertens hårda dom efter mötet
articles.summary: De rödgröna partierna har träffats, men regeringsfrågan diskuterades aldrig. S, V, C och MP verkar exakt lika oense som de var för en månad sedan, bedömer statsvetaren Tommy Möller.
articles.body_text: De rödgröna partierna har träffats, men regeringsfrågan diskuterades aldrig. S, V, C och MP verkar exakt lika oense som de var för en månad sedan, bedömer statsvetaren Tommy Möller. – Jag kan inte se att det har rört sig framåt ett dugg, säger han. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. S, V, C och MP möttes på Lidingö för första gången efter valet, men diskuterade inte regeringsfrågan. Statsvetaren Tommy Möller anser att partierna fortfarande är lika oense som före valet. På måndag ska Magdalena Andersson rapportera till talmannen. Statsvetare bedömer att det är sannolikt att hon kommer att begära mer tid. På fredagen samlades Socialdemokraterna , Vänsterpartiet, Centerpartiet och Miljöpartiet på konferenshotellet Högberga gård på Lidingö. Det var partierna första gemensamma möte efter valet. Under dagen fick partiledarna lyssna på föredragningar från olika samhällsaktörer om Sveriges utmaningar. Men den stora frågan – hur partierna ska kunna enas om en regering – avhandlades aldrig . – Vi har inte alls pratat någonting om regeringsförhandlingar i dag, sa C-ledaren Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist efteråt. Enligt Tommy Möller, professor i statsvetenskap vid Stockholms universitet, verkar partierna fortfarande stå lika långt ifrån varandra som de gjorde innan valet.

articles.title: Fredspristagarens mentor: ”Helt rätt”
articles.summary: Fredspristagaren och advokaten Navi Pillay lärde sig gatans lag av David McQuoid-Mason. Han var hennes mentor och berättar från Durban om deras tidiga äventyr. – Vi satt under ett mangoträd och utbildade unga svarta i mänskliga rättigheter.
articles.body_text: Fredspristagaren och advokaten Navi Pillay lärde sig gatans lag av David McQuoid-Mason. Han var hennes mentor och berättar från Durban om deras tidiga äventyr. – Vi satt under ett mangoträd och utbildade unga svarta i mänskliga rättigheter. Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Så fort David McQuoid-Mason, 83, fick höra att hans adept, kollega och vän Navi Pillay, 85, fått Nobels fredspris började han fundera på hur han skulle fira henne. De lärde känna varandra under tiden då kampen mot apartheid pågick i Sydafrika . – Jag ska spela in en video och skicka den till henne och gratulera. Men sen vill jag göra en sak den 10 december då hon mottar priset. Navi och jag har varit engagerade i ett projekt om en vägg på ett fängelse där olika artister målat motiv med temat mänskliga rättigheter. Men en vit man förstörde väggen och vitmålade den. Navi, jag och andra bestämde oss för att återupprätta väggen och den ska bli klar till december och invigas då. – Jag tänkte att vi ska köra live mellan Durban och Oslo den 10 december, så Navi kan vara med. Professor David McQuoid-Mason var dekan för både universitet i Durban och Howard College Law School och har utbildat alla svarta äldre domare i Sydafrikas högsta domstol. Han är en legend i Sydafrikas juristkretsar. En gång när han träffade drottning Elizabeth gav han henne en Mandelajacka i present – professorn var nära Nelson Mandela och utbildade också presidentens son till jurist. När Navi Pillay kom tillbaka till Durban efter sin Harvardutbildning arbetade hon för David McQuoid-Mason. Han vill prata om hennes goda egenskaper och beskriver henne som känslig, artig och som en mycket god människa.

Det sker kontinuerligt i dag och nu i helgen. Sen får åklagaren ta ställning, säger Olsson Lilja. Enligt kanalen företräder toppadvokaten Elin Ternet en av eleverna. Ternet har haft hand om flera stora fall – hon försvarade en person i ASAP Rockys sällskap efter hans gripande 2020. articles.title: Trumps ilska mot Nobels fredspris
articles.summary: Den sydafrikanske juristen Navi Pillay tilldelas Nobels fredspris. Något som gör Donald Trump arg. ”I dag har Nobelkommittén dragit skam över sig själv bortom all räddning”, lyder ett Truth Social-inlägg mot Trump delat.
articles.body_text: Den sydafrikanske juristen Navi Pillay tilldelas Nobels fredspris. ”I dag har Nobelkommittén dragit skam över sig själv bortom all räddning”, lyder ett Truth Social-inlägg mot Trump delat . Ljuduppspelningen är AI-genererad. Felaktigheter kan förekomma. Pillay får priset för sina ”insatser för att främja fred och internationell rätt”. 2025 ledde hon en FN-utredning som pekade ut Israel för folkmord i Gaza. Valet av Pillay har väckt stora reaktioner, bland annat från israeliskt håll. En annan som rasar är Donald Trump. Presidenten har flera gånger i år hävdat att hans arbete för fred i världen borde belönas. Ett par timmar efter Nobelkommittén presenterade sitt val delade han ett inlägg på Truth Social. ”Pillay är en uttalad motståndare till USA och Israel. Under sin tid på posten hyllade hon terrorister och belönade Hamas”, lyder inlägget. På sin presskonferens möttes Pillay av stora applåder, och passade på att dela ut en känga till Trump. – Om ni klappar lite till kanske jag delar det med Trump, sa hon skämtsamt. Förra årets pristagare, María Corina Machado, delade senare sitt pris med Trump och gav honom till och med medaljen. Inlägget som Trump delat fortsätter med att kritisera Pillays position kring konflikten mellan Israel och Hamas.

articles.title: Kan nobba festen: ”Är inte Bob Dylan”
articles.summary: Nobelpristagaren i litteratur, poeten Anne Carson, 76, firar priset med att boxas i Reykjavik. Men om hon kommer till prisutdelningen, det vet hon inte.
articles.body_text: Nobelpristagaren i litteratur, poeten Anne Carson, 76, firar priset med att boxas på MMA-gymmet Mjölnir i Reykjavik. Men om hon kommer till Stockholm för prisutdelningen, det vet hon inte. Hon har viktiga åtaganden och är uppbokad. – Vi har andra saker vi lovat göra i december. Så jag vet inte. Vi har inte löst det än, säger Anne Carson. Gårdagen var som vilken dag som helst hemma hos paret Carson på Island. Pristagaren svarar inte i telefon om hon kan slippa, inte ens dagen då Nobelpriset i litteratur basuneras ut över världen. – Anne visste inte ens om att det hände. Hon fick fem samtal under frukosten från ett nummer hon inte kände igen så hon svarade inte, säger maken Robert Currie, 75, konstnär och ”kollaboratör” som hans hustru kallar honom. – De ringer från Sverige. Borde du inte ta det? undrade Currie. – Jag svarar aldrig i telefonen på morgonen, säger Carson. Men till slut gav hon med sig, och orden som redan fått vingar över världen var det enda som yppades: ”jag lyssnar på vinden”. Anne Carsons känsla när hon pratat med Akademiens ständige sekreterare under torsdagen: – Nej, inte riktigt. Jag tycker fortfarande att det är galet, säger hon. – De angränsar till varandra, eller hur? Lyssna på vinden. Det låter typiskt som något en poet skulle säga. Men platsen vi möts på är allt annat än luftigt poetisk, köttig och kraftfull snarare. En stor byggnad märkt med en gigantisk torshammare, gymmet Mjölnir, där Carson boxas på fredagar. För ett par år sedan drabbades hon av Parkinsons. Det är sjukdomen som fått henne att börja boxas, och det hjälper henne.

articles.title: Mohamed Ali (V) kommer till riksdagen på måndag | Expressen
articles.summary: Den 13 september går Sverige till val. Följ Expressens direktrapport med senaste nytt inför valet.
articles.body_text: V-politikern Mohamed Ali, som kontroversiellt kryssade sig in i riksdagen i Borlänge, kommer närvara i riksdagen på måndag, uppger han på Ekot. Ali förekommer i en pågående polisutredning om otillbörligt verkande vid röstning, men har inte delgivits misstanke. Vänsterpartiets ledare Nooshi Dadgostar säger också att mötet var bra. – Nu går processen framåt och jag utgår ifrån att vi under de kommande dagarna får se en process som kommer närmare en regeringsbildning. Det är kontexten. Vi behöver se till att en ny regering snart kommer på plats. – Det är Magdalena Andersson som har ett sonderingsuppdrag. Talmannen har gett henne i uppdrag att bilda en ny regering. – Nej, men det är i den kontexten det här (mötet) kommer i. Vi har pratat med varandra och de aktörer som var på plats. Centerpartiets ledare säger att mötet varit bra och att partierna nog dragit olika slutsatser av läget för Sverige. – Jag tror att vi har väldigt olika bilder. Olika reflektioner kom upp efteråt. Det är klart att det är viktigt att vi kan sitta ner vid samma bord. Vi kan prata och utbyta erfarenheter. Men de ekonomisk-politiska talespersonerna och gruppledarna träffas ofta. På frågan om partierna kommit överens om något under dagen säger hon: – Nej vi har inte kommit överens om något i dag.
